k-1.x_notes: Clean pages that follow the format: header, footer, and five numbered problems with large boards at actual size (1-inch triangle edge checked). Every figure works: the sailboat (11 triangles) and cat (7) take any pieces; the hexagon and 2x2 diamond can each be filled several ways; the arrow takes 2 chevrons and the six-point star takes 3 (checked); the 1-2-2 long hexagon takes 5 blues; the side-3 mountain takes 9 greens. The tasks are clear and concrete. Weakness: several fills are quick (the sailboat, the cat, the single-hexagon fill), so a capable first grader may run out of work before forty minutes. There is little invention or open-ended challenge.
k-1.y_notes: Same problems and diagrams as X, plus things the organizer objects to: a 'Shape Detectives!' title and 'Today you'll become a shape detective' intro, a 'Great job! You're a tiling superstar!' placed before any work is done, a printed hint for the chevron problem ('Start at the pointy tip...'), and a 'Bonus Challenge' heading over Problems 4-5. That heading marks the last page optional, which encourages the K-1 group to stop early, the exact complaint about K-1 sheets ending too soon. Nothing is added that helps the children.
k-1.reason: The mathematics is identical, but Y adds cutesy text, a hint, and a 'Bonus Challenge' label that makes the last page look optional. X is already the clean version the organizer would end up with after editing Y.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strong development of kernel 1. Problem 1 has possible and impossible boards (B and D can be tiled; A and C cannot). Problem 2 is the side-2 to side-5 triangle packings, leading to 'n empty spaces' and 'explain why you cannot leave fewer'. Problem 3 compares blues with chevrons on six boards; the results check out (B: blues 0 empty, purples at least 4; F: blues 2, purples 4; the arrows tile fully with both). The question 'can you cover one purple with blues' sets up the chevron-implies-blue argument. Boards are at actual size. Small weaknesses: both impossible boards in Problem 1 have odd area, so the even-area obstruction first appears only in Problem 2. 'Problem 2' is repeated as a heading on its continuation page. There are several record-the-count prompts.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Same content as X, with damaging additions. Problem 2 says 'Hint: Color the triangles that point up and the triangles that point down, then count each kind', which gives away the central discovery of the band. A 'Fun fact: Mathematicians call this kind of argument a coloring proof!' box takes the place of the answer line under the final explanation question. Also a decorative 'The Great Board Mystery' title and a 'tiling isn't just about filling space, it's about seeing hidden patterns!' line (the 'not X but Y' tic). A layout overflow produces a blank fifth page with no header.
grades-2-3.reason: The problems are identical, but Y's hint gives away the coloring argument that is the whole point of the band, and Y adds a fun-fact box, a decorative title, and a blank overflow page. X can go to class essentially as is.

grades-4-5.x_notes: A well-built kernel 2 sequence on the 1-2-2 hexagon, a board on which children physically place blocks, printed at actual size. It asks for all 6 tilings (8 recording boards provided), then the flip map, shortest route, and odd-return parity. Ribbon codes follow, with 2 L and 2 R so C(4,2)=6 matches the six tilings. The page then rebuilds tilings from ribbons and finds the rule that a flip swaps an adjacent LR pair. The mathematics is correct and the worked ribbon example is helpful. Weaknesses: ten numbered problems, several of them small, with some 'record/compare' steps. Problem 7 already leans toward a directed sequence.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Same diagrams and sequence as X, plus a 'Welcome, tiling explorers! ... secret world of flips' opener and a 'Part 2: Ribbons, the Secret Code' heading. 'Explain your thinking.' is tacked onto Problems 2 and 3. Problem 7 is rewritten into directed steps (a)-(d) that end with 'Look at how many edges the board has on its left and right sides', which prints the method and gives away the explanation. All of these are what the organizer's standard rules out.
grades-4-5.reason: The mathematics is the same, but Y adds a cutesy welcome, a decorative section heading, boilerplate 'explain your thinking' lines, and turns Problem 7 into step-by-step directions with the key idea given away. X is cleaner and leaves the discovery to the children.

overall.reason: The two packets share the same problems, diagrams, and correct mathematics in every band. Y's only differences are additions the organizer has said he does not want: cutesy titles and praise, hints that give away the central ideas (the up/down coloring, the ribbon-length explanation), a 'Bonus Challenge' label that invites K-1 to stop early, a fun-fact box replacing an answer line, and a blank overflow page. X is ready to use with little or no editing; Y would spend his fifteen minutes per band on deletions just to get back to X.
